RAILWAYS, CANALS AND TELEGRAPH LINES   CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present the motion that the first report of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, presented to the house on Wednesday, February 1, be now concurred in.

maintopic: RAILWAYS, CANALS AND TELEGRAPH LINES   CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
For
reasons which I set out on Friday in regard to a similar motion for concurrence in the report of the committee on banking and commerce, I desire to oppose this motion.
I do not propose to reiterate the reasons given on that occasion. I think it is sufficient if I have permission of the house to make reference to what was said in that debate, and to say that I still find myself opposed to the proposition that a committee chairman can come before the house and ask concurrence in a committee report which recommends that the committee should have leave to sit while the house is sitting, without at the same time giving the house any reasons why that particular committee needs such an extraordinary right.
As far as I know this particular committee has no special business indicated for its attention this session, and in the absence of any such circumstance I find myself opposed to the motion for concurrence; that is, opposed to paragraph 3 of the report. I note that in paragraph 2 a request is made to reduce the quorum of this particular committee from 20 to 10, again without any particular reasons being given, but I do not particularly raise that matter at this time.
I therefore move, seconded by my colleague the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier):
That the motion be amended by inserting the words "paragraphs 1 and 2 of" after the word "that" and before the word "the".
The motion would then read:
That paragraphs 1 and 2 of the first report of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines be now concurred in
The significance of the amendment in this form is that the other parts of the committee's report would be concurred in, and if the amendment were carried it would merely mean that the paragraph having to do with the right of the committee to sit while the house is sitting would not be dealt with today and that matter would stand in suspension in so far as the house is concerned.

speechtext:
That is exactly what I said. I point out the fact that we realize very well that with the number of committees set up it is sometimes difficult for hon. members to be present in all of them, particularly so if those committees sat while the house is sitting. However, this has become the traditional course. Objection has been taken in the past, and I seem to recall that when I was in opposition similar arguments were advanced.
I also recall, however, that when it came to the implementation of the power given by the house, then as now this course was not arbitrarily followed. Every consideration has been given to hon. members by the committee to the end that hon. members will not be placed in an impossible position.

Railways and Canals Committee
I simply raise the question because that has been the practice in the past, and no harm that I know of has resulted under that practice. I am sure that every care and consideration will be exercised by the chairman and members of the committee to the end that injustice or inequity should not be allowed to occur, and to the end in particular that hon. members shall not be denied the fullest opportunity to be present in the house.
Sometimes when this question is raised it occurs to me that although hon. members have a very strong desire not to have committees sit while the house is sitting, the attendance of hon. gentlemen in this house is not always what it should be. It is no different in this house from the situation that obtains in the British House of Commons. All hon. members are not present throughout the full day. After the orders of the day have received attention those hon. members who are particularly interested in subjects coming before the house remain in attendance. I am sure that no injustice would be done under this arrangement.
Sometimes we hear it said that our members are not present to the degree that they should be, that more of them should be in the house. That has been said throughout the years. I was impressed upon reading Friday's issue of the London Times to learn that on Thursday in the House of Commons in the United Kingdom it was found that there was not a quorum present. When the matter was brought to the attention of the speaker those who were in the environs came in and the house proceeded. The fact that hon. members are not always present but have other work to do in no way indicates their lack of interest and responsibility.
That being so, I am sure that much of the argument to the effect that there would be gross interference with the rights of private members, in the event that this motion was passed, tends to disappear in the light of experience.

maintopic: RAILWAYS, CANALS AND TELEGRAPH LINES   CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Perhaps I might be allowed to say one word in connection with the matter. The objection taken by the hon. member for Ottawa West had to do with two committees only, the one last week dealing with banking and commerce and the other this week dealing with railways, canals and telegraph lines. The objection taken in connection with both was that it seemed to him and to us that the over-all powers should not be taken at this time because in these committees, and more particularly in the one now before the house, the matters dealt with normally are bills of a public or a private nature, where it is not necessary for witnesses to remain in attendance on the committee over a period


of hours or even days. In my experience, at least, most of the time they have been witnesses from government departments, principally from the Department of Transport or its agencies. Surely it cannot be said that it is difficult for these witnesses to come here.
Therefore it seemed to us, as I am sure it seemed to the hon. member for Ottawa West, that this was a power which should not be given until later on in the session. If there should come a time when witnesses were required to remain here for several days, then a request could be made for the power. It seemed to us that this power should not be asked for now because it is not necessary. This is a matter which I at least would like to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister.

maintopic: RAILWAYS, CANALS AND TELEGRAPH LINES   CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I should like to say that the committee we are discussing today has a great deal to do with the national development of Canada. If the hon. member for Laurier will cast his mind back he will recall that a great many bills of one kind or another, having to do with the development of Canada from one end of the country to the other, come before this committee. There have been occasions when witnesses have been brought here and if the sitting had extended over several days it would have entailed considerable personal sacrifice and expense on the part of these people. Therefore I do not think we are at all out of order in asking for this privilege.
As I say, this is not something new; it is something that has been done before. I suggest that the house accept this motion. I can assure the house and the committee that we will not abuse the privileges that are being given to this committee by this motion.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: STATEMENT ON MANUFACTURE OF MAIL BOXES AND KEYS IN PENITENTIARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) asked certain questions regarding the repair of mail boxes, and I am now able to reply.
In order to provide work in connection with the rehabilitation and training of prisoners, post office street letter boxes and relay boxes have been repaired in penitentiaries, principally Kingston penitentiary, for many

years and certainly since the 1900's. Only the metal work has been carried on in the penitentiaries; no locks were repaired there and no keys officially manufactured.
However, late in 1956 Post Office Department officials received an indication that keys might have been secretly manufactured in Kingston penitentiary and smuggled out. As a result discussions took place with the penitentiary officials, and my department received assurances from them that protective measures would be taken.
Recently certain mail box thefts were committed with illegally manufactured keys, and my officials informed me that keys were again issuing from Kingston penitentiary despite the protective measures which had been taken there. This was the first indication I had been given of this problem, and as a result it has been decided to discontinue mail box repairs in penitentiaries and have the work done by commercial firms.
I have given consideration to changing the locks on mail boxes but have decided against this step at this time, because there are over 40,000 such boxes spread across Canada and the estimated cost would be in excess of $200,000, and there would be no effective increase in security. The type of professional criminal who is able to procure a key and use it to open mail boxes will not be deterred by a change of locks; even bank vaults and safes are not always proof against their ingenuity. Furthermore, in most cases where mail boxes have been rifled the box has been forcibly broken open and no key has been involved at all.
Perhaps I might be permitted to say a few words more, Mr. Speaker, on a closely related subject. It has been post office practice for a number of years to pay rewards to those giving information leading to the arrest and conviction of persons who have committed offences concerning the post office. A similar practice is followed by the Canadian Bankers' Association and other organizations.
Some of these organizations have publicized their willingness to pay these rewards and have found it helpful. Until now the Post Office Department has not done so, but we will shortly be issuing a poster for display in all post offices offering rewards of from $200 to $2,000 for information leading to the arrest and conviction of those guilty of various types of offences against the post office and the mail it carries.
The two actions I have referred to today, Mr. Speaker, indicate that while it may never be possible to eliminate thefts, robberies and burglaries completely, aggressive action is being taken by the government to prevent such occurrences and to apprehend and convict those responsible. One measure
Housing
of our success in this regard has been demonstrated by the fact that the number of robberies in the nine months ending December 31 has decreased from 292 in the previous year to 248 in the current year, and our losses of cash and postal supplies from such robberies dropped from $135,557 in the same period of the previous year to $87,042 for the current year.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN LOANS AND HOUSING STARTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement I wish to make has nothing to do with awards. Because of the swift and vigorous response of the house building industry to actions taken recently by the government and the resulting very significant impact on unemployment, I wish to make a brief statement.
All hon. members will, I know, be happy to learn that total National Housing Act lending activity in January was higher than in the same month for any other year in the whole history of N.H.A. activities. Loans were requested during the month for 3,515 dwelling units. This figure compares with a mere 157 in January, 1960, and with the previous high of 3,192 in January, 1958.

Housing
Of the 3,515 units, 1,460 were by approved lenders compared with 151 a year ago and 1,580 in January, 1955, when the banks had their first full year of lending under the National Housing Act, 1954. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation financed the balance of 2,055 units. Although most of the January loans were to home owner applicants and to builders who had already obtained purchasers, a feature of the month's lending was the $8,135,000 approved for 961 units of limited dividend rental accommodation for lower income families and elderly persons.
I must report also that the rising trend in new housing starts, unbroken since last August, continued in January, the increase being 4.7 per cent over the same month a year ago.
Finally, I revert to December, 1960, which was a near record month for home improvement loan activity. This, of course, reflected extension of these loans to rental properties, including apartment houses. Home improvement loans during the month amounted to $4,683,000, the highest dollar volume since September, 1958. These figures indicate, Mr. Speaker, the immediate effects on economic activity and employment of some of the amendments to the National Housing Act were made in December last.

PAYMENT OF BENEFITS TO WIDOWS OF CANADIAN WORKERS
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this house the government should consider the advisability of amending the Unemployment Insurance Act so that any benefits to which a Canadian worker would have been entitled be made available to his widow.
(Translation):
He said: In introducing this resolution, it is advisable to read the notice of motion. We find then that those concerned by the resolution now under discussion are the needy mothers. The notice of motion reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Unemployment Insurance Act so that any benefits to which a Canadian worker would have been entitled be made available to his widow.
That idea, Mr. Speaker, was suggested to me by one of my constituents who had obviously discussed the matter with his fellow workers. It is as a result of some practical experience that this idea sprang up in the minds of those workers.
As long ago as the first session of this parliament, I had the opportunity of discussing this matter briefly when I took part in the throne speech debate.
I shall refrain from saying again what I stated at that time, but I should like to refer my hon. friends to page 347 of Hansard of May 22, 1958.
Subsequently, every year since 1958, I put on the order paper the resolution I have just read. As you know, Mr. Speaker, according to the rules of this house, if a resolution is

not among the first six ones to be drawn, it stands no chance of being discussed during that same session. That is what happened in 1958, 1959 and 1950.
But in 1961, in the course of this session which started in November, I placed this motion on the order paper the very first day. It happened to draw number three, which gives me an opportunity to deal with it more fully today and go into more detail than I did in my outline of May 22, 1958. May I point out immediately that this proposal is in line with the general policy of the Liberal party in the field of social security. That is so true that I am going to quote to you right now paragraph 5 of page 28 of the new statement of Liberal policy made in 1958:
Extend unemployment Insurance benefits to as many people as possible.
Well, you are quite aware, Mr. Speaker, that eligibility for unemployment benefits is not transferable in case of death. The heirs cannot expect to receive any more than what is owed to the deceased in the week of his death.
You know, Mr. Speaker, that the death of the head of a family always brings tragedy in the family, because he leaves a widow and children behind him, and sometimes quite a number of children. The death of the father leaves his family without a breadwinner. Such a tragedy, of course, causes more hardship in the working classes because it is in those classes that people live from hand to mouth.
It is of the utmost importance that a family should have minimum resources to carry on for a while after the death of the breadwinner. As you know, Mr. Speaker, a certain amount of time must elapse after a decease, particularly in the case of the head of a family, before the estate can be settled, and it sometimes takes up to six months. And during that time, bank accounts and other properties belonging to the estate are temporarily frozen under both federal and provincial succession duty legislation.
And the widow and children are sometimes forced to borrow large sums of money at heavy interest to take care of their needs.
It is true that there are provincial workman's compensation laws and also laws providing assistance to mothers in need. But here again, for a case to be processed by the workmen's compensation board, in instances where death is the result of an accident, it takes time, and the widow has no money to 90205-6-111
Unemployment Insurance Act live on in the meantime. In the case of a mother in need, the inquiry by the provincial officials takes from three to six months, and I hardly need to stress the plight of the mother during that time.
The suggestion I am making today, on behalf of the people of the Megantic riding, would cover that period of time and provide the people concerned with a minimum of money to live in the meantime. Then, under what circumstances could those benefits be obtained? Evidently, the present terms of the act will continue to apply. In the case of a labourer or a wage-earner, the application will be dealt with according to section 25 of the act, which defines the insured occupations. It would also be necessary to establish whether the benefits are regular or seasonal. That is not too important, for all you would have to do would be to look up the file of the individual concerned to determine whether he is entitled to regular or seasonal benefits.
If the head of a family dies as a result of an accident, of illness or an accident sustained on his job, I submit that even then it is not too important because the general provisions of the act would still apply.
If the widow is getting benefits under the workmen's compensation act, she would of course have to declare her earnings to the unemployment insurance commission, and if such earnings exceed the amount permissible under the Unemployment Insurance Act, she would not in such a case, be entitled to unemployment benefits. But if, on the other hand, her incbme is below the permissible amount she could obtain the difference allowed by the Unemployment Insurance Act.
In the case of death following an illness, it would be necessary to establish whether the illness started while the individual was unemployed, or even whether it was the cause for the separation from employment. There again, the general terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act would apply, and people claiming benefits would have to comply with the other provisions of that act.
If death resulted from an accident other than an occupational accident, the solution would be easy. The widow could then apply for and obtain unemployment insurance benefits.
Now, for how long should the widow be entitled to such benefits? At present, the act provides for 52 weeks of regular benefits, while seasonal benefits are available only for the period comprised between December 1 and May 15.

The act could operate normally and the benefit period could depend on the number of weekly contributions standing to the credit of the deceased breadwinner.
Mr. Speaker, those are the main reasons why I feel that the draft resolution under review today should receive the support of all members, regardless of whether they sit on this side of the house or on the government side.
. The benefits payable under such circumstances would cause no extra drain on the unemployment insurance fund, since only a small percentage of the people of this country would be entitled to them.
In closing, I urge my hon. friends to allow this resolution to be adopted by the house today.

subtopic: PAYMENT OF BENEFITS TO WIDOWS OF CANADIAN WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this house is asked to express an opinion. If we accepted the resolution proposed by the hon. member we would be recommending that the government give consideration to amending the Unemployment Insurance Act in such a way as to give a widow whatever benefits a deceased worker was entitled to receive.
It is a resolution which appeals to our better qualities. It is sentimental. I do not doubt in the least that people would go along with that suggestion, with that idea, in the proportion of ten to one. It no doubt appeals to the Canadian worker, as it is intended to. If the Canadian worker is concerned with anything he is concerned about the financial position which his wife would have to meet in the event of his death. Though he might be a spendthrift and live from hand to mouth and day to day he would still be in favour of this idea, because a dollar, no matter from What source, is a welcome addition to the security of his widow.
This resolution is intended to appeal to the widows of workers, and no doubt it will. There is hardly a woman who does not live from day to day in fear of losing the breadwinner of her family, of losing her mate, of losing her loved one. Above all she worries about the financial condition in which her family would find itself in the event of her husband's death. This house should commend the hon. member for having conceived the idea contained in the present motion. Although he does not claim full paternity of it I still give him credit for bringing the idea to the attention of the house. We should not be


human, we should not be Christian, if we did not admit that the idea behind this resolution is a Christian one.
However, the hon. member for Megantic has made reference to some of our statutes which provide for security to widows. I wish to elaborate on them, and to say that the idea is not a new one. Every province has statutes which are intended to assist destitute widows, in particular widows who are left with children. We have provincial workmen's compensation acts, which provide for compensation to widows whose husbands lose their lives in the course of their employment. We have the wives' and children's maintenance acts. We have a child welfare act in Manitoba under which the state provides for the needs of a widow left with children. Rights to benefit are conferred in Ontario under the statute known as the mothers' and dependent children's allowance act, which provides for such contingencies. Nor do the federal statutes fail to make provision for destitute widows or widows who require assistance. I refer hon. members in particular to the war widows' allowances act. That is as far as it goes.
I fully realize that unless a widow qualifies under these statutes she cannot receive assistance. That is why the hon. member's idea is a commendable one. A widow could be left penniless on the sudden death of her husband; she might not even have enough money to meet the funeral expenses. Even if her husband does leave an estate, I admit that it does take time to obtain letters of administration or letters of probate from our courts before she has access to whatever resources may have been left.
The concept behind the hon. member's resolution appears to be that a widow should receive at least the sum to which her husband would be entitled under the Unemployment Insurance Act. That seems to be the crux of the matter embodied in the resolution. I ask the hon. member this question. Is there anything in the Unemployment Insurance Act which gives a workman entitlement to any particular or definite sum?
I listened very carefully to the introductory remarks of the sponsor of this resolution. He omitted to indicate to the house whether an amendment of the nature he suggests would fit in with the principles of the Unemployment Insurance Act, or whether it would in effect pervert its principles. I am led to wonder whether such an amendment could be incorporated into the act or whether it is based on a false conception, a false hope that anything and everything is possible, that all you have to do is throw responsibility on the government and condemn the government for not carrying it out even if it is impossible to carry it out.

I hope that hon. members who participate in this debate will give some thought to the questions I have posed and answer them if possible. For my part I submit that the hon. member has placed an erroneous and false interpretation on the Unemployment Insurance Act. This legislation is not social welfare legislation. The hon. member believes that an amendment under which the worker's benefits under the act could be transferred to his widow is compatible with this legislation, but he has failed to prove this and I see no possibility of it being proved. It is true that this legislation has been so frequently amended and its interpretation stretched to the breaking point that those who brought it into being would today scarcely recognize the original intentions behind the measure. I am in full accord with the intention of the hon. member, but he has built his case on erroneous premise.
I trust that hon. members will follow me in this analysis. What I have in mind is this. Under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act a worker, qualified for benefits, is entitled to receive them when he is unemployed. For the purposes of this illustration let us say he is qualified for 20 weeks of benefits at $15 a week. Under the legislation he is not entitled to 20 x $15, or $300, but is entitled to weekly benefits based on weekly reports he must make. If he obtains employment within a three-week period he will have drawn $45, but he has no legal claim on interest in or right to what he may have anticipated receiving, i.e., the balance of $300. On the basis of the premise adopted by the sponsor of this measure the worker, regardless of having found employment, would be entitled to the full $300 and could transfer that entitlement to his widow, his estate, his heirs or to whomever he pleased. If that premise were correct, of course, the hon. member's amendment embodied in this resolution would fit like a glove.
I submit that under the Unemployment Insurance Act a worker is not entitled to any certain sum. He knows what his weekly benefits will be and he knows for how many weeks he qualifies to draw unemployment insurance benefits, but he has no legal claim to any specific sum nor can he draw benefit when what is coming to him has been exhausted.
In my submission the Unemployment Insurance Act is not social welfare legislation but straight insurance, and in no way differs from, let us say, fire insurance or automobile insurance. Both those forms of insurance offer protection. The Unemployment Insurance Act offers protection to a worker in the event of the loss of his job. His entitlement to that 90205-6-llli
Unemployment Insurance Act protection is based on his contributions. Until circumstances are such that the insured under a fire insurance policy can make a claim to the company, he has no interest in the fund set aside by the insurance company to pay claims when they arise. The same situation obtains in the case of an automobile insurance policy. An insured pays his premiums but has no interest in the fund set aside by the company to meet contingencies until the insured is involved in a collision or in some other way damages his automobile.
Under fire and automobile insurance policies however, an insured is entitled to cancel his protection at any time he chooses and receive a refund of the premium he has paid. You cannot do this under the Unemployment Insurance Act. If you stop making contributions you cannot ask for a refund, because you have absolutely no interest in the unemployment insurance fund. I am not losing sight of the fact that under the provisions of this act and its regulations, out of every dollar in the fund the worker contributes five twelfths, the employer five twelfths and the federal treasury two twelfths. I should like the hon. member to explain to what portion, if any, the worker is entitled during his lifetime. I am afraid that in his introductory remarks he did not take note of that; he ignored it entirely, intentionally or otherwise.
As I have said, this resolution is very appealing; it is bound to appeal, and I think that is the hon. member's intention. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that the worker has no interest in the unemployment insurance fund to which he has contributed, none whatsoever, except on the happening of a certain event. The first event is that he has to be without a job, but under the act it is not sufficient just to be without a job. That was the principle on which the act was first built; that was the original intention of the creators or fathers of this particular legislation. First, as I said, there must be the happening of a certain event, namely that he is without a job; but that is not sufficient. There must be more, and what is that? Everyone knows that he must register, be capable of and available for work during all that period of time to which he is entitled according to the provisions of the act. By no stretch of the imagination can we say, Mr. Speaker, that a man who is sick-he may be available-is capable of work, and even less so when he is dead. But even when he is available and capable he cannot tell from week to week how much of a drain his unemployment will be on the fund. There is nothing definite, nothing certain, Mr. Speaker, and there is

Unemployment Insurance Act nothing left for the widow when he dies. Therefore this resolution is built on a permise without foundation.
The Unemployment Insurance Act is a straight insurance act with a contract being the guiding principle all through it. I have an illustration I should like to give the house. Suppose it has been determined that at the time the worker makes his claim he is entitled to a maximum of $30 per week for 12 weeks, or a total sum of $360. Has he any entitlement to this amount when his claim has been approved? Should he be unemployed for 12 weeks, certainly he will draw the $360; but if he should, as I have already mentioned, secure employment within four or five weeks, then that is all he is entitled to and that is all he will get. If he gets a job he is not entitled to any benefit. Oh, I know there are mistaken impressions and mistaken interpretations of this act throughout the country. I think every hon. member realizes that there are abuses. As I said before, this act has been amended so often that its original creators would hardly recognize it, but insurance is the main principle on which it is based.
I could give the house an example of a man or a woman who has contributed to the fund for 34 years while working at a permanent job during that time, but is required, to retire at 65 on a sizeable pension. Yet this person has the mistaken idea that because he or she has contributed to the fund for 30 or 40 years, he or she is entitled to withdraw at least the money put in, and if he or she can get more, all the better. But the act says they have to register, and they register. The next step is to be available for employment, but who wants to employ a man of a certain age who has been discharged or pensioned off by others? Through technicalities there are many people who are drawing unemployment benefits for 52 weeks. I submit that this idea would fit in wonderfully well with some portion of social legislation.
I posed certain questions to the hon. member which he did not touch on, much less try to answer. There would be a considerable drain on the fund, but the hon. member has not indicated how collections would be made or whether workers would be asked to increase their contributions. He has attempted really to create another breach in the battle that we are carrying on to defend the integrity of the fund, because to carry out this suggestion would mean a considerable drain on the fund.
I will admit that this is a good idea; it is attractive; it has a sentimental appeal, but it does not fit into the Unemployment Insurance Act. It fits in no better than a square peg in a round hole. This idea could be the subject of new legislation altogether.

My sympathies are with the widow who is left penniless and needs money in a hurry, but we already have some legislation in that direction. I like the Ontario legislation that I have already mentioned. With respect to mothers' allowance legislation, it could be amended to take in the widow regardless of whether she has children of a minor age. I think this could be the subject of a special statute. I appreciate the value of this suggestion, but I submit that it does not fit into the concept of the Unemployment Insurance Act because, as I have said, there is no sum to which the worker is entitled even when he is qualified for benefits.

subtopic: PAYMENT OF BENEFITS TO WIDOWS OF CANADIAN WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Megantic on bringing this very important problem before the house today, but I am afraid that right at this moment I must part company with him because this resolution is not a very good solution to the important problem that he has brought before the house.
I am also afraid that the resolution shows a woeful lack of imagination on the part of members of the Liberal party, in that once again we see them taking a fund designed for one specific purpose and trying to spread it across the whole gamut of all the social problems with which we are faced today. Let us take a look at the resolution. It reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Unemployment Insurance Act so that any benefits to which a Canadian worker would have been entitled be made available to his widow.
As the hon. member for Marquette pointed out in what I think was possibly a legal interpretation, the worker is not really entitled to any benefits unless he falls within a certain set of circumstances. I am not going to go into the legal aspects of the matter at all, because I do not think we have to do so. I should like to consider for a moment just what the resolution means. Is a widow only going to be entitled to whatever unemployment benefits her husband may have on his death? Is that the way we are going to solve the problem of widows in this country? Certainly, Mr. Speaker, we need a fund for widows, but not the unemployment insurance fund.
I think this resolution points up one of the reasons why we find the unemployment insurance fund in the predicament it is in today. If we cast our minds back to when the fund was originally established we will recall that it was set up for a specific purpose, on the simple theory that while a person was working he would pay a premium which would

give him at least a subsistence payment when he was temporarily out of work.
What has happened to this principle over the years? We have seen it steadily eroded through political expediency, through use being made of the fund's vote-catching possibilities which neither the Liberals nor the Conservatives apparently are able to resist. The principle of the fund has been extended far beyond its original scope. It has been extended to take in people whom it was never intended to cover under the original principle of the plan.
What has this brought about? It has created a public contempt for the fund from coast to coast. People see other people drawing benefits from the unemployment insurance fund to which in fact they were not entitled under the original plan, so they say, "If they can get it, why can I not get it"? As a result the fund has developed into a great and bottomless pork barrel into which everybody is trying to put their hand. We see it extended to business, to government, to pensioners and to the public generally, with everybody trying to get in on the act.
I had occasion not too long ago to try to establish a disability pension for one of my constituents who is afflicted with a steadily creeping paralysis. His employer, one of the mines in my riding, kept him on as long as he could possibly get to work, and they leaned over backward to try to keep his job open. When he finally reached the stage where he could no longer go to work and we were trying to obtain his disability pension, a government official advised him not to take it until his unemployment insurance benefits had run out.
Was the fund designed for that purpose? Are we supposed to care for our disability pensioners out of the unemployment insurance fund? Are we supposed to maintain our old age pensioners out of the unemployment insurance fund? Or should we establish a fund for these pensioners that would be adequate to provide them with at least a decent living?
The impression I got from the hon. member for Marquette was that we have an adequate system of social security plans without having to dip into the unemployment insurance fund. I do not accept that statement. If we did have such a system I do not think we would have this resolution before us today. In my opinion the only reason the resolution is before us is that there is a very definite need in this field, in that in many cases widows in this country are in very desperate straits. That is why the hon. member has brought this resolution before the house, and I commend him for at least that aspect of the thinking behind it.
Unemployment Insurance Act
I think we should face up to and accept our responsibilities as members of the house to try to provide some solution for this problem. However, as I said before, so far as the unemployment insurance fund is concerned I think we should return to unemployment insurance principles. I do not think there is any other piece of legislation on the statute books today that comes in for as many complaints across the country as does the unemployment insurance fund.
We hear cries from here and there that we should police the fund and try to do away with some of the many abuses that are being perpetrated against it at the present time, but I should like to say that policing is no answer. If we were to police the fund adequately we would need a police force larger than the number of civil servants we have today. The only answer I can see is some kind of massive educational program to get the Canadian people back on the right track so they will realize what the fund is for and will use it in that light.
I think it is time we did something to counteract the fallacy that has been built up in this country of a great benevolent father government granting funds to deserving children from some strange and mysterious source. I think it is time we told the Canadian people that the strange and mysterious source from which they get these funds is their own pockets and nowhere else.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the last two speakers have indicated, there would appear to be general support for the suggestion that widows in this country should be adequately provided for. However, that it should be done by means of the Unemployment Insurance Act is, of course, not as acceptable. For one thing, as the hon. member for Timmins has pointed out, it would not provide adequate protection for them to any extent and, second, such action would be absolutely beyond the concept of the Unemployment Insurance Act. In raising this matter at this time I think the hon. member for Megantic has directed our attention to what should be contained in the Unemployment Insurance Act and how it should operate.
The hon. member for Timmins has had a good deal to say about returning to unemployment insurance principles. However, in discussing this matter with people generally across the country I find that everyone has a different idea of what are unemployment insurance principles. For instance, the hon. member for Marquette compared unemployment insurance to some extent with fire insurance. I suppose a great many people have that idea, that it does compare with that in principle. However, there are many different features in unemployment insurance as compared with fire insurance. For instance, it would not make any difference whether a man had made only one premium payment to the fire insurance company; if his house burned down he would receive the entire amount of money necessary to rebuild it. The Unemployment Insurance Act has never operated in that way, because the benefits a man receives are directly contingent upon what he has paid into the fund. His own protection is related to his accumulation of credits. I do not believe that this should be the case.
Unemployment, of course, has been a serious threat to the workingman of this country, and indeed throughout the world, for over 600 years. He has struggled during the course of that time to promote legislation which will give him adequate protection against unemployment. I can only say I would be opposed to bringing anything else into this act until such time as every employable person in the

labour force of this country is given adequate protection when he is unemployed through no fault of his own. This has not been done up to the moment. It is true that the present administration has made great steps forward in providing improved protection. However, the protection is not yet complete, because we have many people who are not covered by the act at all.
If the fund is going to be drained by people drawing out of it unnecessarily, then individuals are not going to be provided for properly. One of the things for which labour has struggled throughout the years has been recognition of the fact that a man who is unemployed through no fault of his own should be in a different category from those who are suffering other forms of hardship. During the long history of the unemployed this has been a difficult thing to achieve. As far back as 1300 there was unemployment and for 300 years after that time, generally speaking, the unemployed were treated as criminals. Then for the next 300 years they were treated generally as paupers.
During this century, in most countries in the world we have made some great advances in providing protection for unemployed men. However, the unemployed man has never achieved the main principle which I believe should be accepted, and that is that a man has a right to a job. He has the right to a job or he has the right to adequate compensation for the loss of that job. I envisage the Unemployment Insurance Act, therefore, as working generally in the same way as the workmen's compensation act works. Under that act a person is compensated for the loss of his job through injury. I can only say that as long as a person is ready, willing and able to work and is in the labour force, I believe he is entitled to compensation from society if he should lose his job through no fault of his own.
When we consider the great many ways in which a man can lose a job through no fault of his own we can begin to realize just how important a proposition this may be. The most outstanding example of this, of course, and the one about which we hear most these days, is automation and technological improvements. This is one way in which a man can lose a job through no fault of his own. Perhaps the decline or decay of his trade may be another example, or the bankruptcy of his employer. There are thousands of ways in which he can lose his job through no fault of his own. When he loses his job his family suffers hardship because, under the present set-up, when the man's benefits expire he then goes on some form of unemployment assistance. This means that he is required to meet a means test. He may

lose his home and his assets, all the things for which he has worked during a lifetime, by reason of a situation which is beyond his own control.
I do not believe this should be the case. I therefore believe that the present act, instead of being opened to take in other groups as suggested in this resolution, should go forward and provide adequate protection for every employable person in this country. I believe that can be done very easily without causing any strain on the fund or upon the taxpayers of this country.
If the kind of benefits I suggest were provided, of course, there would need to be some limitations placed in the act. I would think the main principle to be incorporated in this act should be that a man is entitled either to a job or to adequate compensation if he is out of work through no fault of his own. I believe that every employable person in the labour force who is employed should contribute to the fund, regardless of his income or occupation. I say that because at the moment the contributors to the fund seem to be mainly those who are unsteady workers, and those who are steady workers seem to be left out. I think the civil service is a good example of this. The civil servants say, "We should not have to contribute to this fund; we work steadily and we are not out of a job." There are many civil servants, however, who are out of a job, civil servants who are employed on a seasonal basis.

We do not even know, and we are not able to ascertain, whether she is willing to work, because in some instances there are not jobs to offer and it is a very difficult thing to determine whether a woman is actually out looking for work. I believe in this way the resolution before us today has a very direct bearing on the Unemployment Insurance Act, because provision for widows could in large measure be obtained by life insurance. That would be a more adequate and proper form of insurance through which to protect widows. However, the workingman in this country is not at all times able to provide adequate life insurance. It is one of those things he hesitates to take on because it is a payment he must meet every month. While he is working he may well be able to make those payments. However, with the uncertainty of employment hanging over his head all the time, he hesitates to take on those payments to provide for his wife and family, even though he could afford to do so if he were working all the time.
Therefore if we were to put ourselves in the position where we could ensure that the workingman of this country was going to have an adequate income, whether he was

Unemployment Insurance Act employed or unemployed, then he would be in a much better position to provide that kind of insurance for his family. He would know that his income was not going to stop entirely, or that he was not going to have to meet a means test which might require him to give up all his assets before he was entitled to receive benefit payments.
That is why I believe there should be some limitations upon the act. Again, I think, there are many other people drawing out of the fund unfairly. For instance, take the case of a seasonal worker. He pays into the fund for perhaps eight months. He may earn a considerable income in those eight months because, generally speaking, those employed in seasonal industries earn higher wages than those in the other fields of employment, because of the very fact that their employment is seasonal.
I was just taking a look at this publication, "Employment and Payrolls" for September, 1960. It shows that the average wage in Canada, according to the industrial composite, is $76.57 per week. However, that is only a national average, and when we come to consider the individual industries there is quite a large variation. For instance, in the mining industry the average wage is $93.50 a week. On the other hand, in service industries the average wage is $53.16 a week. There is quite a difference; that is almost half the average weekly mining wage.
So in actual fact a person might well be in a seasonal industry and earn as much in eight months as a worker in a different industry might earn in 12 months. It would be most unfair that the one man should pay into the unemployment insurance fund for 12 months while the other man who earned perhaps a greater salary in the eight months he worked should draw benefits out of that fund for four months.
For that reason I suggest there must be a limitation placed upon the amount which a man can earn and still draw from the fund. All these kinds of things are necessary if we are going to provide adequate protection. I believe that providing an adequate level of income for the workingman would overcome many of the other difficulties in which he is placed, including this one that has been brought to our attention today, of making adequate protection for his widow. Therefore I suggest that rather than dragging other people into the fund at this time we should place a limitation upon the amount of wages a man can earn and still draw benefit from the fund.
For the purpose of setting forth these principles that I think should be contained in the act I have used the figure of $4,000. The reason I use that figure is that it is

just on the national average that I have already outlined. The national average weekly wage is $76.50. Four thousand dollars per annum, which is the figure I have suggested as a limit for the purpose of setting forth the principle, amounts to $76.90 per week.
It is obvious that here again a uniform payment across the country would not be fair or reasonable and it may have to be set on a regional basis, because when we come to look at the various areas in the country it can be seen from this same publication "Employment and Payrolls," September, 1960, that the average wage in British Columbia is $83.66 per week. On the other hand, in Prince Edward Island it is $53.72 per week. Therefore I think it would be unreasonable that the ceiling should be the same in Prince Edward Island and British Columbia. That would have to be taken into consideration in enacting the principles I have suggested. Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the speeches made by the hon. member for Megantic, the sponsor of this resolution, and the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, who spoke in support of it. I welcome this resolution because it serves to highlight a problem we have in Canada. It underlines the fact that we do not have a comprehensive social security system in this country. I regret that history has shown that we adopt our social security system by bits and pieces. Over the years new items of legislation have been introduced, but even today we realize that many people deserving of consideration on the part of society are not receiving the required consideration.
I have examined the social security systems in other nations of the western world. Only the Netherlands has a system that is more complicated and piecemeal than ours. In most nations of the world the problem of social security has been tackled in one fell swoop.
I regret that I must oppose the resolution now before us because it is a violation of the basic principles of the Unemployment Insurance Act. May I underline the word "insurance". I give the sponsor of this resolution full marks for having regard for the widows of men who die while they are enjoying unemployment insurance benefits. However, may I ask the hon. gentleman what consideration he would give those widows after the expiry of those benefits? After all, we know there is a limit to the number of months a man can enjoy benefits under this legislation. Worthy as her cause may be, to appeal on behalf of the widow for only those limited months during which her deceased husband would have been in receipt of unemployment insurance appears to be most inadequate.
If we had a transferrable, portable pension plan as advocated by hon. members of this group over the years, and if we had a comprehensive social security plan we would not have to worry about the idiosyncrasies of existing legislation. We would not have, in the light of important national problems, to move resolutions of relatively minor importance even though they may be of major significance to the individuals involved at the time. I am rather disappointed that a spokesman for the Liberal party attempts to involve this house in a day long debate on a minor resolution having to do with only one of our social security laws in order to obtain benefits for a very limited number of people. We in our group humbly submit that the time of this house could be

Unemployment Insurance Act put to better use and even the attendance in this house might be greatly enhanced if we were to engage in an all-out campaign to replace the existing piecemeal legislation that we now have with an over-all basic social security law.
We have pensions for the blind; we have pensions for the handicapped; we have old age pensions; we have pensions for those over 70; we have pensions for veterans; we have pensions for the burnt-out veterans; we have pensions for the youngster aged from zero to 16; we have pensions for this and pensions for that, each with its fantastically costly overhead and administration. I am sure if we analysed what the taxpayers of Canada are paying for social security at the present time, with all the overhead, all the red tape and the paper work involved, together with the means tests and all the rest of it, and compared that with the cost of a basic, comprehensive social security system as they have in the United Kingdom and in most of the other western nations of the world, we would realize that we are heading in the wrong direction with our little amendments here and our new acts there to look after another little category and the whole hierarchy of administration involved. I believe we would easily recognize in our investigation that we should offer to our people a basic minimum standard of living at a much lower cost. Therefore, we feel this is wrong in so far as the basic principle is concerned. It is also a violation of the intent of the Unemployment Insurance Act to introduce the amendment of-ferred in this resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a word on this resolution which no doubt has a great appeal to the Canadian people in general and more especially to the humanitarian aspect which is found in all of us. During the course of the debate this afternoon something was said about the danger that would arise in introducing changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act which, if the intent of the resolution is accepted, would place an additional drain on the fund.
The hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) favoured the establishment of a separate fund to take care of widows. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in order to appreciate the intent of the resolution one should have an understanding of the Unemployment Insurance Act which was introduced in 1941 by a Liberal government. Under this act unemployment insurance is contributory and each of the contributory groups, that is, government, employer and employee, has a direct interest in the insurance fund. In dealing with individual claims the rights of all contributors must be considered. The receipt of a benefit is a statutory right of the claimant who has met the required conditions. In other words, when an insured person makes a claim he is asking for something to which he is entitled and is not asking for a gift. It is a right which cannot be attacked even by a court of law. By that I mean that it cannot be denied in any way or be subjected to garnishee by a court of law.
The moneys in the unemployment insurance fund may be used for only two purposes, namely for those who are rightly entitled to make claim for benefit and, second, by way of a refund of contributions if contributions were made in error. To be entitled to a claim for benefit, therefore, one must have been a contributor and establish proof of a contribution record of not less than 30 weeks. Another condition required is that the individual demonstrate that he is capable of and available for work but unable to obtain work that he can perform.
The suggestion contained in the resolution that the benefits legally due to a claimant based on his record of contributions be paid to his widow may be contradictory to the basic principles on which unemployment insurance was conceived. However, the resolution does not presume that upon the death of the insured the benefits would be paid to his widow if the employee had not been drawing unemployment insurance at the time
Unemployment Insurance Act of his death. The widow would only be entitled to the benefits until entitlement is exhausted.
It can be argued that if such an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act as would conform with the intent of the resolution were to be made it would be a precedent which, if extended, would ultimately impose a still greater drain on the fund which is now dangerously near being depleted without the assumption of additional burdens. Notwithstanding the fact that the widow could not be deemed to have made any contributions to the fund, nor could the interpretation be that she would have assumed the place of her deceased husband in the labour market, the benefits which she would receive under this amendment would be very modest indeed.
I fully realize that every insured person under the act is issued an insurance number for life. The number is not transferable and upon the death of the insured it is retired and never again used by anyone. The number, therefore, is positive identification which gives the insured person the right to benefit.
In spite of all the objections which have been raised this afternoon I would urge hon. members to examine the resolution carefully in the light of the humanitarian aspect of its intent, and I wish to commend the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) for introducing a measure for the consideration of the house which, if approved, would give a little lift to some of those who have suffered that irreparable loss which no material benefits can possibly replace.

subtopic: PAYMENT OF BENEFITS TO WIDOWS OF CANADIAN WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to express briefly my views on the subject dealt with by this resolution. I assume that the mover, knowing how often widows are left in difficult financial circumstances, wishes to assist at least those whose husbands are entitled to benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I, too, well realize the need. I know of many cases where widows are in very needy circumstances, where the husband was unable for one reason or another, to provide for his widow. Indeed I know of many cases where the husband was unable to provide for his own funeral expenses.
Some may feel that this is the man's own fault if he did not make this provision while living so that his widow and family would be provided for after his death. There may be cases where this is true; but, generally speaking, when a man fails to provide for his widow it is because he was unable to do so. Even if no provision was made through the man's own fault because he may have been a spendthrift, as was suggested by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk), that does not alter the fact that the widow is in real need of assistance. Therefore I think that the object which this resolution seeks

to obtain is a worthy one and one which will meet with general approval.
I think we should realize that husbands, especially those in the lower income group, just cannot always make adequate provision for their wives and children because the income they earn must be used for the maintenance of the home and family. So that too often, and much too often, men die and leave their widows in desperate financial circumstances. I am referring to those who do not leave estates, as was referred to by the sponsor of the resolution in his remarks.
This is true not only when, unfortunately, a young man dies leaving young children, but it is also true of older men whose families have grown and have established homes of their own. I realize, of course, that in many cases some provisions are made by governments. If a man dies, leaving children under 16 years of age, the widow will receive mother's allowance from the provincial authorities until the children are 16 years of age. This has already been mentioned by some previous speakers. If the widow is 65 years of age she can receive old age assistance. There is also workmen's compensation, and so on.
But there are many who do not qualify for any of these benefits. If they are in need they can only apply for assistance under the social assistance act where this is in effect. I know that in my own province of Nova Scotia this is only paid if the municipality has agreed to share the cost, and certainly in Nova Scotia they have not all done so. Even where it is paid it is not the answer. There is still the idea of receiving public charity; there is no certainty that it will continue to be paid. I believe widows deserve better from their country. I think they should have that peace of mind, that feeling of security, which a pension gives when they receive assistance as a matter of right, not as charity and not as a favour.
Let us examine the situation which faces many women when their husbands die. At such a time there is always a need of money and often there is none. It is a time of severe emotional distress. Many adjustments have to be made, and it is at this most difficult time a widow has to face financial distress and make many difficult decisions. I know that younger women, if they have had special training before marriage, can often return to work. One sees them working as teachers, nurses, stenographers, office clerks and the like. But for a woman over 50 years of age it is another matter. She has spent her adult life as a homemaker. There is no possibility of employment for her; she has none of the skills or training necessary for a position in business or industry.

Personally, I believe the Canadian people have an obligation towards these widows, an obligation we should recognize and fulfil.
The amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act proposed by this resolution would not solve the whole problem. Yet it would be of some assistance to many widows, and it is for this reason I support it. I well realize it would not assist those widows whose husbands did not come under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Further, it would not help those whose husbands had used up their benefits, and these in all probability would be in a worse financial position than widows whose husbands had not drawn such benefits. Again, if a man prior to his death had been receiving benefits there might be very little left for the widow to receive.
I well understand also that the Unemployment Insurance Act was not designed to make the proposed payments, to widows; it was not meant to be life insurance. Indeed, it is more in the nature of sickness or accident insurance. I suppose some people feel that since they have made contributions under the Unemployment Insurance Act, perhaps for many years, and received no benefits, their widows should receive them. I do not think this would apply any more than one would expect to get back premiums under an accident policy if one did not have an accident.
I think if this amendment were adopted there would have to be an increase in the contributions made by employers and employees, and there may be considerable opposition to this. Perhaps it is not practical to amend the act as this resolution seeks to do. As to this I express no opinion. If it can be done and I repeat, if it can be done, I would suggest that all widows of men who made contributions be treated equally and that any benefits received by the husbands be disregarded. I would further suggest that all such widows receive a lump sum payment or a weekly payment regardless of whether the husbands had received benefits, or, indeed, had exhausted their benefits under the act.
I think the mover of the resolution has performed a very useful service in bringing this problem to the attention of the house. It serves the purpose of focusing the attention of this house on the gap, as it were, which exists in our social security system. We do not have provision for the widows left in poor circumstances I have mentioned. Indeed, we do not have provision, either, for those older unmarried women who are without adequate means of support and who do not qualify for any of the various pensions now in effect. I believe the Canadian people would welcome the opportunity to make pro-
Unemployment Insurance Act vision for pensions for those unmarried women who need assistance, or who will need assistance long before they would qualify for old age assistance. I hope it will not be too long before provision can be made so that those widows and those unmarried women I have mentioned will be receiving some form of pension. The need is there, and the need is great.
In any event, the proposal before us would, if adopted, give needed assistance to some widows at least.

The resolution with which we are dealing today is one which I believe should be considered from every possible angle, because I am of the opinion that all members of this house are sincerely concerned about any situation where a widow finds herself in financial difficulties as a result of the loss of the family breadwinner.
Most of us at one time or another have witnessed the very difficult circumstances in which some widows find themselves. I know we all feel very strongly that various means should be provided in order that these financial difficulties might be in some way alleviated. Fortunately the financial situation does not always present the same degree of hardship. As has been mentioned today there are various provisions for the assistance of widows. Some hon. members have mentioned widows' allowances, which are available if financial circumstances prove them to be necessary. I believe this is a very worth-while social measure. Other hon. members have pointed out that compensation is sometimes available. We must, of course, remember that generally compensation is only available if a death occurs as a result of injury or accident, in which case it is doubtful whether the Unemployment Insurance Act would be effective anyway because in a great many of these compensation cases death is caused while the person concerned is on the job in which case, of course, there would be no eligibility for benefit under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I notice one interesting point about this resolution. The hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) who proposed it specifically mentioned widows. As I say, that is commendable, and he is to be congratulated for having brought it to the attention of the house. However, there are many cases in close relation to this subject, which should, possibly, be given equal consideration. One that occurs to me is the case of a widower qualified to receive benefit, dies and has one or more small children. I think the situation there would be of the same nature as the one we have been considering, and the situation would perhaps
1772	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance Act be more difficult than the situation of a widow left with small children. Of course, there are many cases where as the result of the husband's inability to work due to physical handicaps the woman of the family is the only breadwinner. In the event of her death, if she were drawing unemployment insurance benefits at that time, you would have a widower who is unable to work and possibly dependent small children. I notice that these cases have not been taken into consideration in this resolution and it is a cause of some wonderment to me why this eventuality should not have been included.
This resolution-as is the case with one or two provisions now included in the regulations under the Unemployment Insurance Act-is in the nature of a definite departure from the original concept of unemployment insurance. The original idea which I think should be stressed and applied was unemployment insurance benefits for those people who through no fault of their own are out of work and available for work. The concept embodied in this resolution is a departure from that. As I said, some of the regulations under the act are in themselves a departure from the original intention of the legislation.
If we examine the regulations carefully I believe we will find that people who were drawing unemployment insurance benefits and are committed to hospitals or mental institutions probably through no fault of their own are still able to draw benefits and of course they are not available for work during that period of time.
The act is primarily designed to provide benefits to those who for reasons beyond their control have become unemployed but who are available to accept employment. Appealing as may be the subject matter of this resolution I am afraid I cannot agree with the hon. member for Megantic that the unemployment insurance fund should be used for social welfare measures of this nature. I believe that financial assistance should be made available to widows where proved necessary in order to assist them to avail themselves of opportunities for adequate training to allow them to accept work in many of the fields where work of a certain nature is available.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir), many widows in Canada today are accepting employment in business establishments and stores. Some who were previously registered nurses are again taking up this vocation. Some are accepting employment in secretarial work and many others as teachers. In some cases I have found that they are very anxious to get into their line of work as quickly as possible.


Although I do not believe the unemployment insurance fund should be used for social welfare I reiterate that some assistance should be available to widows to allow them to take special training so they may avail themselves of work that may be available.
Over the years a great deal of criticism has been levelled at the present government by the opposition in regard to the present state of the unemployment insurance fund. I have definite opinions about the contribution made to the depletion of the fund by measures such as the one we are discussing at this time. Although I feel that the amount in the fund should at no time be the determining factor as to whether widows should be entitled to receive the benefits to which their deceased husbands would have been entitled, I am wondering why a measure of this nature is introduced at this time by an hon. member supporting a party that, when it formed the government and as a result of an economy not of its making, had the fund built up to a lofty figure and still did not consider at that time that it was necessary to bring in a measure such as the one before us for consideration today.
The plight of widows in financial straits today is no different from that of widows during the past 20 years and so I am wondering why this measure is being introduced at this time when all hon. members of this house are vitally concerned with the condition of the fund. I do not believe that the unemployment insurance fund is the means by which parliament should increase the social welfare benefits which must of necessity be increased in Canada and because I feel this is not the avenue we should follow in this respect I cannot support this resolution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson). I felt that his closing remarks relating to the depletion of the fund were highly appropriate and pertinent in the discussion of this resolution. At the same time, like the hon. member for Churchill, I agree that this resolution contains much merit. The group of people it is designed to assist represent a classification that presently does not come under the fund and certainly consideration should be given to that question in this light. However, as the hon. gentleman pointed out, the idea behind this resolution is more in the field of welfare than in the field of insurance and should therefore be considered from that point of view.
In the past few years the unemployment insurance fund has been extended to assist groups and classifications of unemployed in fields not previously considered, including

fishermen and seasonal workers. This has placed the fund in a state of imbalance which has resulted in moneys being expended that were not accounted for when the original contributions were fixed as between employees, employers and government. As a result, great concern for the present state of the fund is being shown today by employees :hroughout the country.
In the light of these facts it is my opinion that consideration should be given to the set-ing up of a second fund, if that were feasible, in which could be placed such groups as seasonal workers, fishermen, farm labourers and possibly also married men who are seeking re-training in skilled occupations. Possibly this fund could be subsidized by the government, because all of these groups making contributions to it could not maintain it. Also possibly a percentage of the regular unemployment insurance fund could be used to help finance this second fund. However, I do believe that the significant amount that would have to go into it should come necessarily from the general revenue of the country. Everyone appreciates the problems that must befall the widow at the time of her husband's passing. I can think of nothing that is more tragic and no greater responsibility that is placed on a woman in her lifetime than in the losing of her husband.
It has been said that there are other means available to widows in those circumstances. However, we in government, I think better than anyone else, appreciate the red tape that is associated with any welfare payments that are available to the public. Certainly I will agree that in circumstances such as these civil servants make a determined effort to cut the amount of red tape to a minimum but red tape still exists. There are delays as well that make it most difficult, I would think, for a widow who was the wife of an ordinary wage earner, whose income through the years had been used up in providing the necessary essentials of life, leaving nothing available in the way of an estate to his family when he passed away. In these circumstances I would think that a payment such as is proposed in this resolution would be a Godsend to the wife for it would assist her to get over that period when things are most trying and allow her the opportunity to complete the necessary forms to enable her to qualify for other schemes which are available to her.
I cannot imagine how we could consider this as a proper type of measure to fall under unemployment insurance, as it was originally set up to establish protection for workers who through no fault of their own find themselves unemployed. It is a different type of scheme. Possibly the seasonal worker could also be considered to be not strictly within the original confines of the act and maybe the
Unemployment Insurance Act fisherman as well. Along with the fisherman, there is no reason why the agricultural farm labourer should not be in the same position.
All of these things seem to fit into a specific sphere that it was not the intention of the Unemployment Insurance Act originally to cover, but many of them do come under the act at the present time. If we were to place widows under the Unemployment Insurance Act we would just be going further in the direction that we find is causing us a great deal of difficulty today. What we must do is give consideration to a different scheme, something that will look after these most worthwhile categories but will not deplete the present fund beyond the point it has reached already.
Like the hon. member for Churchill, I wonder why the Liberal member did not bring this to the attention of his party and why they did not give consideration to it when they were in power. Certainly they were in power at a time when the fund was at a much higher level than it is at the present time. Undoubtedly it would have been much more feasible to undertake it at that time; that is, if they were considering this type of legislation or this type of individual. The fact is that probably the hon. member realizes that there has never been a government in power in Canada that has had a more humanitarian approach to the ordinary person in this country and more willing to listen and try to do something about the problems confronting the ordinary citizen than this government. Certainly, he was wise to bring this resolution before the house because he is sure, as are the widows of this country, that they will receive from this party and this government every possible consideration that can be given in the light of the existing situation.
