Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a word on this resolution which no doubt has a great appeal to the Canadian people in general and more especially to the humanitarian aspect which is found in all of us. During the course of the debate this afternoon something was said about the danger that would arise in introducing changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act which, if the intent of the resolution is accepted, would place an additional drain on the fund.
The hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) favoured the establishment of a separate fund to take care of widows. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in order to appreciate the intent of the resolution one should have an understanding of the Unemployment Insurance Act which was introduced in 1941 by a Liberal government. Under this act unemployment insurance is contributory and each of the contributory groups, that is, government, employer and employee, has a direct interest in the insurance fund. In dealing with individual claims the rights of all contributors must be considered. The receipt of a benefit is a statutory right of the claimant who has met the required conditions. In other words, when an insured person makes a claim he is asking for something to which he is entitled and is not asking for a gift. It is a right which cannot be attacked even by a court of law. By that I mean that it cannot be denied in any way or be subjected to garnishee by a court of law.
The moneys in the unemployment insurance fund may be used for only two purposes, namely for those who are rightly entitled to make claim for benefit and, second, by way of a refund of contributions if contributions were made in error. To be entitled to a claim for benefit, therefore, one must have been a contributor and establish proof of a contribution record of not less than 30 weeks. Another condition required is that the individual demonstrate that he is capable of and available for work but unable to obtain work that he can perform.
The suggestion contained in the resolution that the benefits legally due to a claimant based on his record of contributions be paid to his widow may be contradictory to the basic principles on which unemployment insurance was conceived. However, the resolution does not presume that upon the death of the insured the benefits would be paid to his widow if the employee had not been drawing unemployment insurance at the time
Unemployment Insurance Act of his death. The widow would only be entitled to the benefits until entitlement is exhausted.
It can be argued that if such an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act as would conform with the intent of the resolution were to be made it would be a precedent which, if extended, would ultimately impose a still greater drain on the fund which is now dangerously near being depleted without the assumption of additional burdens. Notwithstanding the fact that the widow could not be deemed to have made any contributions to the fund, nor could the interpretation be that she would have assumed the place of her deceased husband in the labour market, the benefits which she would receive under this amendment would be very modest indeed.
I fully realize that every insured person under the act is issued an insurance number for life. The number is not transferable and upon the death of the insured it is retired and never again used by anyone. The number, therefore, is positive identification which gives the insured person the right to benefit.
In spite of all the objections which have been raised this afternoon I would urge hon. members to examine the resolution carefully in the light of the humanitarian aspect of its intent, and I wish to commend the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) for introducing a measure for the consideration of the house which, if approved, would give a little lift to some of those who have suffered that irreparable loss which no material benefits can possibly replace.

Unemployment Insurance Act feel that we must look not only at the specific words but at the benefits in general that are paid out of the unemployment insurance fund. In effect this resolution would introduce a new class of persons who would draw benefits from the fund. I should like to say that for a member who has placed the same resolution on the order paper on past occasions I thought that while his motives may have been sound and sincere he did a somewhat inadequate job of introducing the resolution. I feel that he could have clarified it much better and advanced many more arguments in favour of the resolution than he did.
For example, certain questions came to my mind immediately when I read the resolution. How long would the widow be entitled to draw benefits? Would she be entitled to draw them for the same period that her deceased husband would have been entitled to draw benefits? Would she be entitled to draw benefits for life? What would happen in the case of a man who died say next Monday and would have been laid off next Tuesday and thus be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits? What would happen to his widow? Would she be entitled to draw benefits? Where would the dividing line be drawn? If the widow is entitled to draw benefits for life, are we not in fact setting up a new pension scheme paid for by the taxpayers of this country? I feel that all of these questions should have been explained to us by those who advocate that this resolution be passed.
The hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) also mentioned that this resolution is in accordance with the general policy of the Liberal party. This was a rather frightful statement when we realize that those who were placed in a position to draw seasonal benefits by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) are responsible for some of the depletion of the fund today. Now we have a member of the Liberal party attempting to add another class of people to those entitled to draw from this fund, thus further depleting it. The hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) adequately pointed out that we must be concerned about the cost not only to the fund but to the contributors to the fund, the taxpayers of the country, the employees and employers of the country.
I was very pleased to hear the remarks made by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin), for whom I have a regard almost equal to his vastness. He mentioned that the fund was designed for one specific purpose when it was originally set up and now, because of Liberal policy referred to by the bon. member for Megantic, we find the fund being spread across all the social problems

with which we are faced today. As a result of this the public of this country, and particularly those who pay into the unemployment insurance fund, have come to think of this fund as an inexhaustible source of money which can be used for almost any reason. Indeed, this is no exaggeration when we look at the abuses that are heaped upon this fund today by employers as well as employees.
I heartily endorse the suggestion made by the hon. member for Timmins that the policing of the fund is no answer but rather that we need a system of education in this country to show the people that they have an interest in this fund and that it should not be abused. We should show the people why the fund should be operated on sound insurance principles for the benefit of the worker and the employer.
I was very sorry that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) was not permitted to continue his argument as to why the widow of a deceased worker should not be allowed to draw from this fund. When a person stands up and says he is opposed to this resolution that may be construed by some as being against any help whatever for widows. I do not believe any member of this house, regardless of where he sits, regardless of what stand he takes on this resolution, could in all fairness be said to be against relief for widows.
However, in considering relief for widows do we not have to go farther than the UnEmployment Insurance Act? Are there not other agencies in this country that have a part to play so far as pensions to widows are concerned, particularly widows of deceased workmen? If you consider the widows of deceased workmen, why not consider widows generally? Do not municipalities have a part to play? Do not the provinces have an obligation? Why must everything come from the unemployment insurance fund? Why set up another drain on the fund? Why should not other methods and means be explored? I, Mr. Speaker, am against this resolution for the reasons that I have outlined and also because I feel this government is possibly more concerned with the unemployed in this country than either of the parties sitting in opposition.
The speech from the throne contained the announcement that amendments would be made to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I believe this government is studying the whole operation of the act with a view to providing a comprehensive program that will embrace not only unemployed persons but those seasonal workers who are not drawing from the fund. This is my hope and my expectation as a believer in sound principles of conservatism. I think there is a great deal

of merit in the suggestion that two funds should be set up. Indeed, there is a great deal of merit in the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kings-way before he was prohibited, under the rules, from continuing his line of discussion.
There are many ways in which we could stop the drain on the fund. What about those who are coming into the labour market today? It has been advocated in some quarters that we should have a program of conscription in order to train the young people coming on to the labour market, and who are not able to find jobs. They would achieve the necessary skills after they had served their term in uniform.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to express briefly my views on the subject dealt with by this resolution. I assume that the mover, knowing how often widows are left in difficult financial circumstances, wishes to assist at least those whose husbands are entitled to benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I, too, well realize the need. I know of many cases where widows are in very needy circumstances, where the husband was unable for one reason or another, to provide for his widow. Indeed I know of many cases where the husband was unable to provide for his own funeral expenses.
Some may feel that this is the man's own fault if he did not make this provision while living so that his widow and family would be provided for after his death. There may be cases where this is true; but, generally speaking, when a man fails to provide for his widow it is because he was unable to do so. Even if no provision was made through the man's own fault because he may have been a spendthrift, as was suggested by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk), that does not alter the fact that the widow is in real need of assistance. Therefore I think that the object which this resolution seeks

to obtain is a worthy one and one which will meet with general approval.
I think we should realize that husbands, especially those in the lower income group, just cannot always make adequate provision for their wives and children because the income they earn must be used for the maintenance of the home and family. So that too often, and much too often, men die and leave their widows in desperate financial circumstances. I am referring to those who do not leave estates, as was referred to by the sponsor of the resolution in his remarks.
This is true not only when, unfortunately, a young man dies leaving young children, but it is also true of older men whose families have grown and have established homes of their own. I realize, of course, that in many cases some provisions are made by governments. If a man dies, leaving children under 16 years of age, the widow will receive mother's allowance from the provincial authorities until the children are 16 years of age. This has already been mentioned by some previous speakers. If the widow is 65 years of age she can receive old age assistance. There is also workmen's compensation, and so on.
But there are many who do not qualify for any of these benefits. If they are in need they can only apply for assistance under the social assistance act where this is in effect. I know that in my own province of Nova Scotia this is only paid if the municipality has agreed to share the cost, and certainly in Nova Scotia they have not all done so. Even where it is paid it is not the answer. There is still the idea of receiving public charity; there is no certainty that it will continue to be paid. I believe widows deserve better from their country. I think they should have that peace of mind, that feeling of security, which a pension gives when they receive assistance as a matter of right, not as charity and not as a favour.
Let us examine the situation which faces many women when their husbands die. At such a time there is always a need of money and often there is none. It is a time of severe emotional distress. Many adjustments have to be made, and it is at this most difficult time a widow has to face financial distress and make many difficult decisions. I know that younger women, if they have had special training before marriage, can often return to work. One sees them working as teachers, nurses, stenographers, office clerks and the like. But for a woman over 50 years of age it is another matter. She has spent her adult life as a homemaker. There is no possibility of employment for her; she has none of the skills or training necessary for a position in business or industry.

Personally, I believe the Canadian people have an obligation towards these widows, an obligation we should recognize and fulfil.
The amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act proposed by this resolution would not solve the whole problem. Yet it would be of some assistance to many widows, and it is for this reason I support it. I well realize it would not assist those widows whose husbands did not come under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Further, it would not help those whose husbands had used up their benefits, and these in all probability would be in a worse financial position than widows whose husbands had not drawn such benefits. Again, if a man prior to his death had been receiving benefits there might be very little left for the widow to receive.
I well understand also that the Unemployment Insurance Act was not designed to make the proposed payments, to widows; it was not meant to be life insurance. Indeed, it is more in the nature of sickness or accident insurance. I suppose some people feel that since they have made contributions under the Unemployment Insurance Act, perhaps for many years, and received no benefits, their widows should receive them. I do not think this would apply any more than one would expect to get back premiums under an accident policy if one did not have an accident.
I think if this amendment were adopted there would have to be an increase in the contributions made by employers and employees, and there may be considerable opposition to this. Perhaps it is not practical to amend the act as this resolution seeks to do. As to this I express no opinion. If it can be done and I repeat, if it can be done, I would suggest that all widows of men who made contributions be treated equally and that any benefits received by the husbands be disregarded. I would further suggest that all such widows receive a lump sum payment or a weekly payment regardless of whether the husbands had received benefits, or, indeed, had exhausted their benefits under the act.
I think the mover of the resolution has performed a very useful service in bringing this problem to the attention of the house. It serves the purpose of focusing the attention of this house on the gap, as it were, which exists in our social security system. We do not have provision for the widows left in poor circumstances I have mentioned. Indeed, we do not have provision, either, for those older unmarried women who are without adequate means of support and who do not qualify for any of the various pensions now in effect. I believe the Canadian people would welcome the opportunity to make pro-
Unemployment Insurance Act vision for pensions for those unmarried women who need assistance, or who will need assistance long before they would qualify for old age assistance. I hope it will not be too long before provision can be made so that those widows and those unmarried women I have mentioned will be receiving some form of pension. The need is there, and the need is great.
In any event, the proposal before us would, if adopted, give needed assistance to some widows at least.

speechtext:
The resolution with which we are dealing today is one which I believe should be considered from every possible angle, because I am of the opinion that all members of this house are sincerely concerned about any situation where a widow finds herself in financial difficulties as a result of the loss of the family breadwinner.
Most of us at one time or another have witnessed the very difficult circumstances in which some widows find themselves. I know we all feel very strongly that various means should be provided in order that these financial difficulties might be in some way alleviated. Fortunately the financial situation does not always present the same degree of hardship. As has been mentioned today there are various provisions for the assistance of widows. Some hon. members have mentioned widows' allowances, which are available if financial circumstances prove them to be necessary. I believe this is a very worth-while social measure. Other hon. members have pointed out that compensation is sometimes available. We must, of course, remember that generally compensation is only available if a death occurs as a result of injury or accident, in which case it is doubtful whether the Unemployment Insurance Act would be effective anyway because in a great many of these compensation cases death is caused while the person concerned is on the job in which case, of course, there would be no eligibility for benefit under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I notice one interesting point about this resolution. The hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) who proposed it specifically mentioned widows. As I say, that is commendable, and he is to be congratulated for having brought it to the attention of the house. However, there are many cases in close relation to this subject, which should, possibly, be given equal consideration. One that occurs to me is the case of a widower qualified to receive benefit, dies and has one or more small children. I think the situation there would be of the same nature as the one we have been considering, and the situation would perhaps
1772	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance Act be more difficult than the situation of a widow left with small children. Of course, there are many cases where as the result of the husband's inability to work due to physical handicaps the woman of the family is the only breadwinner. In the event of her death, if she were drawing unemployment insurance benefits at that time, you would have a widower who is unable to work and possibly dependent small children. I notice that these cases have not been taken into consideration in this resolution and it is a cause of some wonderment to me why this eventuality should not have been included.
This resolution-as is the case with one or two provisions now included in the regulations under the Unemployment Insurance Act-is in the nature of a definite departure from the original concept of unemployment insurance. The original idea which I think should be stressed and applied was unemployment insurance benefits for those people who through no fault of their own are out of work and available for work. The concept embodied in this resolution is a departure from that. As I said, some of the regulations under the act are in themselves a departure from the original intention of the legislation.
If we examine the regulations carefully I believe we will find that people who were drawing unemployment insurance benefits and are committed to hospitals or mental institutions probably through no fault of their own are still able to draw benefits and of course they are not available for work during that period of time.
The act is primarily designed to provide benefits to those who for reasons beyond their control have become unemployed but who are available to accept employment. Appealing as may be the subject matter of this resolution I am afraid I cannot agree with the hon. member for Megantic that the unemployment insurance fund should be used for social welfare measures of this nature. I believe that financial assistance should be made available to widows where proved necessary in order to assist them to avail themselves of opportunities for adequate training to allow them to accept work in many of the fields where work of a certain nature is available.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir), many widows in Canada today are accepting employment in business establishments and stores. Some who were previously registered nurses are again taking up this vocation. Some are accepting employment in secretarial work and many others as teachers. In some cases I have found that they are very anxious to get into their line of work as quickly as possible.


Although I do not believe the unemployment insurance fund should be used for social welfare I reiterate that some assistance should be available to widows to allow them to take special training so they may avail themselves of work that may be available.
Over the years a great deal of criticism has been levelled at the present government by the opposition in regard to the present state of the unemployment insurance fund. I have definite opinions about the contribution made to the depletion of the fund by measures such as the one we are discussing at this time. Although I feel that the amount in the fund should at no time be the determining factor as to whether widows should be entitled to receive the benefits to which their deceased husbands would have been entitled, I am wondering why a measure of this nature is introduced at this time by an hon. member supporting a party that, when it formed the government and as a result of an economy not of its making, had the fund built up to a lofty figure and still did not consider at that time that it was necessary to bring in a measure such as the one before us for consideration today.
The plight of widows in financial straits today is no different from that of widows during the past 20 years and so I am wondering why this measure is being introduced at this time when all hon. members of this house are vitally concerned with the condition of the fund. I do not believe that the unemployment insurance fund is the means by which parliament should increase the social welfare benefits which must of necessity be increased in Canada and because I feel this is not the avenue we should follow in this respect I cannot support this resolution.

subsubtopic: PAYMENT OF BENEFITS TO WIDOWS OF CANADIAN WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson). I felt that his closing remarks relating to the depletion of the fund were highly appropriate and pertinent in the discussion of this resolution. At the same time, like the hon. member for Churchill, I agree that this resolution contains much merit. The group of people it is designed to assist represent a classification that presently does not come under the fund and certainly consideration should be given to that question in this light. However, as the hon. gentleman pointed out, the idea behind this resolution is more in the field of welfare than in the field of insurance and should therefore be considered from that point of view.
In the past few years the unemployment insurance fund has been extended to assist groups and classifications of unemployed in fields not previously considered, including

fishermen and seasonal workers. This has placed the fund in a state of imbalance which has resulted in moneys being expended that were not accounted for when the original contributions were fixed as between employees, employers and government. As a result, great concern for the present state of the fund is being shown today by employees :hroughout the country.
In the light of these facts it is my opinion that consideration should be given to the set-ing up of a second fund, if that were feasible, in which could be placed such groups as seasonal workers, fishermen, farm labourers and possibly also married men who are seeking re-training in skilled occupations. Possibly this fund could be subsidized by the government, because all of these groups making contributions to it could not maintain it. Also possibly a percentage of the regular unemployment insurance fund could be used to help finance this second fund. However, I do believe that the significant amount that would have to go into it should come necessarily from the general revenue of the country. Everyone appreciates the problems that must befall the widow at the time of her husband's passing. I can think of nothing that is more tragic and no greater responsibility that is placed on a woman in her lifetime than in the losing of her husband.
It has been said that there are other means available to widows in those circumstances. However, we in government, I think better than anyone else, appreciate the red tape that is associated with any welfare payments that are available to the public. Certainly I will agree that in circumstances such as these civil servants make a determined effort to cut the amount of red tape to a minimum but red tape still exists. There are delays as well that make it most difficult, I would think, for a widow who was the wife of an ordinary wage earner, whose income through the years had been used up in providing the necessary essentials of life, leaving nothing available in the way of an estate to his family when he passed away. In these circumstances I would think that a payment such as is proposed in this resolution would be a Godsend to the wife for it would assist her to get over that period when things are most trying and allow her the opportunity to complete the necessary forms to enable her to qualify for other schemes which are available to her.
I cannot imagine how we could consider this as a proper type of measure to fall under unemployment insurance, as it was originally set up to establish protection for workers who through no fault of their own find themselves unemployed. It is a different type of scheme. Possibly the seasonal worker could also be considered to be not strictly within the original confines of the act and maybe the
Unemployment Insurance Act fisherman as well. Along with the fisherman, there is no reason why the agricultural farm labourer should not be in the same position.
All of these things seem to fit into a specific sphere that it was not the intention of the Unemployment Insurance Act originally to cover, but many of them do come under the act at the present time. If we were to place widows under the Unemployment Insurance Act we would just be going further in the direction that we find is causing us a great deal of difficulty today. What we must do is give consideration to a different scheme, something that will look after these most worthwhile categories but will not deplete the present fund beyond the point it has reached already.
Like the hon. member for Churchill, I wonder why the Liberal member did not bring this to the attention of his party and why they did not give consideration to it when they were in power. Certainly they were in power at a time when the fund was at a much higher level than it is at the present time. Undoubtedly it would have been much more feasible to undertake it at that time; that is, if they were considering this type of legislation or this type of individual. The fact is that probably the hon. member realizes that there has never been a government in power in Canada that has had a more humanitarian approach to the ordinary person in this country and more willing to listen and try to do something about the problems confronting the ordinary citizen than this government. Certainly, he was wise to bring this resolution before the house because he is sure, as are the widows of this country, that they will receive from this party and this government every possible consideration that can be given in the light of the existing situation.

Mr. Speaker, in opening my remarks I feel it only proper to bring to the attention of the house the experience we had in the province of New Brunswick prior to June, 1957. If hon. members had had the privilege of attending political meetings in New Brunswick and had gone to a Liberal meeting they would have heard appeals from Liberal speakers addressed to the voters in this way: Please, do not vote us out of office or you will lose your unemployment insurance benefits; please do not vote us out of office or a Conservative government, when in power, will take away your family allowances and old age security payments. I believe that since then the people of Canada have been made well aware of the fact that this government believes in social security and social justice. Legislation passed during the past two and a half years should be ample proof of that fact.
1774	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance Act The resolution introduced by the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) has a great deal of appeal to me as a member of parliament from one of the Atlantic provinces. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) put on the record the fact that the average weekly wage in British Columbia is as high as $83, while in the province of Prince Edward Island, according to the latest statistics, it is as low as $52. This fact encourages me to speak in favour of the resolution notwithstanding the fact that it was introduced by a member whose party had an opportunity for many years to introduce this type of assistance.
What I notice about the resolution is that perhaps it does not go far enough. I suggest to the mover of the resolution and to the house that the resolution may not be fair and just to all workers in the country. What about the widower? Should it not apply to him if his wife should die while entitled to benefits? What about single workers, male or female? They often leave unpaid debts when they die and many of them support parents who might be in need of assistance at that particular time just as much as a widow with children. What about a widower, whose wife has predeceased him, who dies and leaves infant children? There are also husbands to be considered, disability pensioners whose pensions are going to be increased but are still not entirely adequate or disabled husbands who because of their disabilities are dependent on wives who are gainfully employed.
All hon. members know that the unemployment insurance commission was established approximately 20 years ago. At the present time there are many local offices and about half a dozen regional offices located across the country. One of the large regional offices of the commission is located in the city of Moncton in the province of New Brunswick. This office serves the Atlantic provinces and because of the fact that large payments must necessarily be made to the residents of the so-called have-not provinces, the existence of unemployment insurance in the Atlantic provinces and in the other less fortunate areas of the country has done much to eliminate hardship and suffering. The existing payments from the fund, more than anything else in the form of social justice, have eliminated hardship, suffering and other unfortunate situations.
It is only in recent years that married women have been allowed to receive benefits. At the present time the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) has a study under way to consider the advisability of including farm labour and agricultural workers as contributors to the fund. When and if the scope of the act is enlarged to allow for this type of 

contributor we will then witness, as we do in the case of seasonal benefits, an additional annual drain on the fund.
At the present time the widows of Canada do not have uniform protection. We have heard mention today of the widow's allowance acts which are provincial statutes. In some of the provinces, particularly the prairie provinces, there are generous disability pensions whether the recipient is a widow or otherwise. Some of the provinces, particularly the four in the Atlantic region, have a maximum of $55 a month for disability pensions whether the person is a disabled woman or a former working man. It is near impossible for these provinces to increase these provincial pensions because of the fact that their revenue from taxation is somewhat restricted.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Smith) criticized the resolution because the mover did not include a time limit during which the benefits might be received. At the resolution stage I do not feel it is appropriate or necessary for the mover to include every aspect of his intentions. However, under resolution No. 44 the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) has certainly given the house a great deal of information as to his intentions. It is unfortunate that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway was not permitted to elaborate in his speech today on the intentions contained in his resolution. However, the principle was placed on the record and at this time I simply want to state that I am opposed to the principle of resolution No. 44 in so far as it would discriminate between residents of the poorer provinces.
Much has been said about the plight of widows. It seems to me that it would be relatively easy and would involve very little expense, if any, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to comply with this resolution. In recent years we have had an increase in old age security. I understand that the fund is almost carrying itself as a result of the amendment of the 2-2-2 formula to a 3-3-3 formula whereby 3 per cent of corporation taxes, 3 per cent of personal income taxes and 3 per cent of excise taxes are made available and allocated to the old age security fund.
By means of a simple regulation or amendment it should be possible to increase by a very small amount and allocate specifically a certain percentage of the contributions paid by the employer and employee in the purchase of unemployment insurance stamps. By doing so many more names might be added to the Martin statistics on unemployment. This could be remedied by putting widows who are not looking for work in a special category.

If the government should decide to implement the resolution, and to separate contributions in so far as widows are concerned, so as and to include these people in a separate category, perhaps at the same time the government should include other recipients in this classification. I suggest students attending technical institutes and vocational schools who can draw benefits although they are not, except by way of a fiction, available for work, and also older citizens in receipt of pensions.
I know a great many Canadian National Railways workers who on reaching age 65 retire on C.N.R. pensions. Because of the fact that they have made contributions to the unemployment insurance fund over the years they are permitted by law, and quite properly so, to draw benefits for a period up to one year. In many cases, however, they do not survive. If this particular type of employee on pension had lived his estate would have been increased in value to the extent of the benefits for one year. If one railway worker can draw benefits for one year while on pension I do not see why it would not be fair in the case of his co-worker who dies that his estate or family should receive similar treatment. I cannot see any difference.
Many workers in Canada have steady work year in and year out. Clerks in stores and office workers find steady work and contribute to the fund while so employed. On the other hand, some seasonal workers only work a minimum of 15 weeks during a one year period, make contributions of less than $1 a week and because of the legislation can draw seasonal benefits for a period of 13 weeks.
This does not appear to be fair in the eyes of the public. As a result, I want to say that I endorse the principle of this resolution and urge the government to implement it. The implementation of this resolution would not add very much to the administrative costs. It would not be necessary for the widows to register every week. They would simply prove that their husbands, had they lived, would have been entitled to benefits, prove the death and draw the amount to which the husband would have been entitled.
While speaking about widows I think it would be proper also for the members of this house to urge the Canadian Labour Congress, boards of trade and other national organizations to encourage amendments to many of the provincial statutes. As I stated earlier, in some provinces the widows are adequately protected by generous payments under widows' allowance legislation or under workmen's compensation. This is not the case in the poorer provinces.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, as a member from the Atlantic area I heartily endorse the
Old Age Assistance
resolution and note that most speakers coming from the poorer provinces have spoken today in favour of it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the adjournment at six o'clock I had the privilege of moving the following resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of extending old age assistance to unmarried women and widows of 60 years of age.
Apart from unemployment, health and hospital care, the area of social welfare

Old Age Assistance
which receives government attention in Canada today has to do with security for aged persons unable to find even casual employment. Of these, the group which has been overlooked is undoubtedly the unmarried woman and widow of 60 years of age and over. During the years that I served as mayor of Fort William I was frequently approached for assistance by individuals, some of whom were out of work, others were incapacitated in some way and unable to obtain or qualify for employment.
Compared with the present time those were prosperous years, but of all these unfortunate people those who looked the most pathetic and who made the greatest impression in their appeal were the women who had reached their sixtieth birthday and were unmarried or widows. Here was a type of citizen who found it most difficult to obtain work anywhere.
I recall the time in 1949 when our telephone system was converted from a manual operation to a dial system, with the result that upwards of 60 women operators were laid off. While the city, which owned and operated the telephone system, gave each a generous severance allowance in accordance with the number of years they had been employed, the older women soon found themselves out of money with no prospects of finding employment in other jobs. These women were unmarried or widows and several of them came to the city hall seeking relief from our welfare department.
I have had this resolution on the order paper for the last two years and during that time I have received hundreds of letters commending this motion. Many of these communications were of a heart-rending nature.
To better emphasize the need and to illustrate my point I have selected two cases which I will endeavour to present in a very brief form. One case concerned a Mrs. A, we will call her, aged 62 who had five children. Her husband, formerly employed as a boilermaker, died after a lengthy illness, leaving $1,500 in an insurance policy, which money was used up to pay funeral expenses and doctor's bills. Mrs. A has since been unable to find employment anywhere, except for odd times as a dishwasher, second cook and baby sitter. Her children are all married and raising families of their own. The only remaining source of income she can look to in order to live is charity or city welfare relief.
The other case to which I wish to refer concerns an unmarried woman of 59 years of age who had been a store clerk and is now working only part time. She is now living on unemployment insurance. She made the statement that she was bom six years

too late, for if she were 65 she could qualify for old age assistance. For a woman to admit that she would rather be six years older than she actually is can only mean that a fearful future is the compelling reason for such an admission.
One of the saddest sights to look at is a destitute woman whose bloom of youth has departed with the years and where the frailty of the human body has visibly set in. As a consequence she is invariably seized with a spirit of dejection the like of which can only be found in people whose creeping despair reflects the extremes of adversity.
In the statements of Liberal policy adopted by the national Liberal convention held in Ottawa in January, 1958, in the resolution on social security there is a provision for the extension of old age assistance to unmarried women and widows of 60 years of age. The critics of this proposed legislation may point out the cost to the government if the recommendations contained in this resolution were to be enacted; it will certainly cost money, but I dare say that with a close examination of the facts it can be done.
I would propose that the present contributions to the universal old age pension fund of 3 per cent of income, 3 per cent of corporation tax and 3 per cent of sales tax, which was increased from 2 per cent to 3 per cent in 1959, be increased to 3J per cent. This would enable the government to not only provide a pension for unmarried women and widows of 60 years of age, but would leave enough to boost the present pension of $55 a month.
At the same time, a higher contribution would have an anti-inflationary effect, thus keeping the value of the pension more stable, and with the development of the country and rise in national production it can be expected that pensions will be increased again in the future.
If and when the government proposes some changes in the old pension scheme, such as the suggestion made by Professor Robert Clark of the University of British Columbia, who made a deep study of the American scheme which is financed by workers and mangement contributions, it would be logical for the government to add the contributory phase so that pensioners could reap the benefit of their own contributions. The introduction of a contributory plan would make possible a reduction from the age of 70 to 65 for men and for women in general to the age of 60.
In any contributory plan, however, pensions should be made portable so that the worker would be able to bring to the new job the pension benefits saved during his or her earlier employment. This would reduce the

pension costs to the new employer and make him more ready to hire the older man or the older woman. I wish to make it clear that by portable pension I mean that all the contributions made by both the employee and the employer are to be transferred from the former job to the new job.
The prospects for the future of our country are much brighter than they appear on the horizon at the present time, and with faith and good management there should be no depression in the vision of Canadians anywhere. Our country is going to grow and increase in wealth beyond the optimist's wildest dream, and it should be our purpose to make life a little bit easier for those who have made their contribution to the sum total of our national heritage and whose fortunes have not been commensurate with what they gave Canada. To these citizens, a reasonable standard of living should be provided by the nation.
Australia, Belgium, Denmark, Greece, Iran, Israel, the Union of South Africa and the United Kingdom; all these countries have set the minimum pensionable age for women at 60, five years lower than the age for men. In countries such as Brazil, the Dominican Republic, France, New Zealand, Paraguay, Peru, the Philippines, Thailand and Turkey, both men and women retire and receive pensions at 60 years of age. In Russia and Japan men receive pensions at 60 and women receive pensions at 55. I have taken these facts from the International Labour Review of October 1955. In 1956 the United States brought the retirement age for women down from 65 to 62, the retirement age for men remaining at 65 in that country. Here I wish to quote from the same review at page 266:
It is very important for the pensionable age to be adjusted to the security needs of older workers, since the essential purpose of old age pensions is to deal with such needs. .. The two main causes of involuntary loss of income on the part of aging workers are loss of ability to work and loss of ability to find a job even while still capable of working. Employment statistics often indicate that women tend to encounter difficulty in remaining in employment at an earlier age than men. Old age benefits have as a purpose not only tne aiding of disabled and unemployed older workers. They should also enable all aged workers, if they wish to enjoy a period of leisure and rest following a long working life, to do so.
In answer to an inquiry sent out by the commission on the status of women of the United Nations economic and social council, one international group replied that some of its affiliates did consider earlier retirement for women, and I quote:
A fair compensation for the special burdens connected with motherhood and care for the family carried by the majority of women, a burden which is particularly heavy for the great mass of women who live in poor economic circumstances.
Old Age Assistance
Since age of retirement has a direct relationship to age of pension, the same reason could be given for women receiving the old age pension at an earlier age.
How can we justify the retirement of air force officers at various ages between 45 and 50 with pensions up to $6,000 and $7,000 a year at a time when most of these men have an opportunity of resuming a gainful career in other fields, while at the same time denying a miserly pension of $55 per month to destitute women of 60 years? I do not criticize a policy which was designed to guarantee certain changes and advancement for men in the services in time of war. I merely wish to call attention to a situation which should be rectified by bringing about a policy more in keeping with the times.
It could also be argued that it is possible to establish flexible pension provisions between pensionable age and retirement age. The method of applying this formula would be a reduction of pension when the person concerned continues to work.
It has also been said unemployment insurance can take care of persons when they are not of retirement age. My answer is that unemployment insurance can only deal with short term periods. Unemployment insurance is not organized to handle the problem of semipermanent unemployment because of age. Hence, old age pension benefits must be adopted to fill the gap.
It must be realized that the principal factor influencing the age at which men or women need pensions should be the difficulty they meet in finding and retaining employment as they advance in age. There is hardly any need for me to re-emphasize the accepted fact that, with the exception of nurses and domestics, women reaching 60 years are the first casualties in the labour market.
This resolution, however, does not recommend a pension for all women of 60 years of age. It limits the benefit to unmarried women and widows. However, I would certainly have no objection if the government would extend the same benefit to all women of 60 years of age regardless of marital status.
In a summary prepared by the United Nations economic council commission on the status of women the suggestion was made that if the age were lowered with respect to the eligibility of women for pensions professional women would be placed at a disadvantage to the point that an employer might be inclined to discriminate against them and dismiss a woman in preference to a man because she would be entitled to a pension. Another point made was that employers might replace older women workers with younger employees who would work for

Old Age Assistance
less wages even though the older women were quite capable of performing their work.
These and other objections are superficial as can be seen from the action already taken by several nations which I have already mentioned. In spite of arguments to the contrary, 19 nations of the world have lowered to 60 the eligibility age of women with respect to pension benefits and no less than 4 countries in the western world are paying pension benefits to women at age 55, namely Italy, Japan, Panama and Argentina. This by no means exhausts the list.
The humanitarian aspect of this resolution is such as should move not only this government but even a heart of stone. Its implementation would bring hope where there is now dejection, would lift the spirit of a human being from the dark recesses of despair to the heights of light and contentment in the declining years of a woman's life.
In conclusion, I express the hope that every hon. member of this house irrespective of where he sits will want to be counted as favouring this resolution not because of any political consideration but because he supports the view that beneath the exterior of a poor, destitute woman beats a heart as noble as any of those whose fortunes enable them to bedeck themselves with the finery which wealth can provide.

That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of extending old age assistance to unmarried women and widows of 60 years of age.

Then as now those women were asking for a pension at 60. Why? Because in most cases, they cannot find employment and in many cases widows, for instance, who have raised large families, are unable to do the work they are offered, I feel that society must assist those needy persons by means of a pension.
Besides, the Liberal party has always been concerned with the welfare of the needy. The social security legislation now on the statute books shows clearly that the Liberal party has always sought to help people most in need of assistance.
Mr. Speaker, during the election campaign of 1958, on February 10, 1958, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) made a speech entitled "Social Security". About old age assistance, he had this to say:
Unmarried women and widows will be able to get old age assistance benefits at the age of 60 instead of 65.
Well, that suggestion, with many others in the Liberal platform, was laid before the electors, but it was not approved by the majority.

Widows and unmarried women will be eligible, starting at age 60, for the pension now being paid to persons aged 65 to 70.
I am happy to see, Mr. Speaker, that an amount of $5,000,000 has been included in the estimates of the Liberal government of Jean Lesage for 1961-62.

The Liberal party in Quebec has found an expression which should certainly please my friend, the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Valade) who does not like the expression "old age pension". Here we speak of "allowances for widows and spinsters aged 60 to 65."

Mr. Speaker, I wish to seize this opportunity to offer my congratulations to the hon. member for having sponsored such a resolution. I am not so good at making a speech and I have no intention of wasting the time of the house by delivering a long one. However these measures are such commendable ones that I would not want to miss this opportunity of congratulating those who have decided at last to take notice of the ills of the people and to present resolutions such as the No. 3 resolution put forward this afternoon

by the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) and the one which is now before the house and which calls for the extension of old age assistance to unmarried women and widows of 60 years of age. Such measures appeal to me.
Speaking as a physician, I may say that in the course of forty years of general practice, I have been witness time and again to the destitution and the extreme poverty not only of unmarried women and widows of 60 years of age but also of widows as young as 40, 35 and often 30.
I have therefore congratulations to extend to the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) and also to the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc) who seconded the motion. However, I have to blame them for one thing and that is for not going far enough.
I agree that we must help those in need. We are here for that. We are here to make laws for the people, to extend to them a helping hand in order not to be beaten in two or three years time by our opponents for having failed to care for the ills and the problems of the people, and for having withdrawn from them.
We want to live up to the excellent reputation which is ours. If we were elected in 1958 by such a great majority, it is because our program took into account the ills of the people. That is the reason why we are members of a government such as this one.
As a physician who sympathizes with the ills of the people, I am happy to say to my hon. friends in the opposition that I am in favour of welfare measures, but I must add: "You do not go far enough. Be more generous." I would suggest, even to the sponsor of the motion to present it again one day and to make it as generous as I would like to see it. In the meantime, I would ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) to go on with the assistance he is already giving, pending this more generous measure that will come from our hon. friends in the opposition. I would ask him to continue to the people the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act amended in 1957, while we are waiting for this more generous legislation that will perhaps be proposed by our hon. friends from the opposition.
I therefore urge them to be generous and bring relief to those aged 60, 40 and 30 years, and more particularly to the widows who, being left without means, with a family to

support, and therefore being unable to work outside, need a generous piece of legislation such as only this government has been able to enact since taking over.
In fact, did this government not, as soon as it took office, raise the old age security pension from $46 to $55 a month, until it is hiked to $75 at an early date. I suggest that this government take this step and at the next general election I shall be happy to ask my government to double, if necessary, for people who deserve it, the rate of old age security pensions and widows' pensions, particularly for those who are suffering hardship because of their age and family obligations, and who are unable to earn a living.
The people will certainly realize and note that while we have no monopoly on social welfare, because politics should not be mixed with welfare, we do have, however, a monopoly on common sense, balance and private initiative. The people will also realize that a government should legislate and govern with the money from the people, with people's money, something we should always keep in mind. We might also recall at this time that the Leader of the Opposition recently blamed us for spending those $500 million of savings put aside by the Liberals when the people had just upbraided the latter for not looking after them. Today he asks us to lead the country into debt through deficits and to help the people.
Well, with all this good advice, you may be assured that I, for one, on behalf of my constituency of Quebec West, and as a medical doctor, have spent all my life trying to relieve human suffering, shall commend my government and urge its members to keep up its splendid policies, its good work for the protection of the poor, the sick, the afflicted, the suffering and the needy.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure everyone must be very sympathetic to a resolution such as this put forward by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai). However, I think there are many questions that should be asked. The hon. member has brushed some of the questions aside as being not fundamental and of no value in any argument. For instance, there is the question that all widows with or without jobs, all unmarried women with or without jobs should have a pension at the age of 60. He brought up this matter of professional women practically forced into retirement at the age of 60, and the employed women whose employers desire younger ladies and may have a very good excuse to put the older women out of work. These are questions that, despite his quick desire to brush them aside as having no meaning at all, should be answered; and I have not as yet heard any answer from the opposition benches.
The hon. member states that the Liberal convention in 1958 first passed this resolution. I am quite sure that if our friends in the opposition thought it would gain them a few more votes they would lower the age to 50 and raise the so-called baby bonus to

Old Age Assistance
40. Therefore we would have a gap of ten years for the New Party to fill up. The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) stated that this was being looked after by the new government in Quebec as no other government in Canada is doing. I think possibly he does not know about our Conservative government in Manitoba. In 1959 they passed an act, one of the sections of which reads:
-the government of Manitoba and each of the several municipalities in the province may take such measures as are necessary for the purpose of ensuring that no resident of Manitoba, including an Indian .. . lacks
(a)	such things, goods, and services as are essential to his health and well-being, including food, clothing, shelter, and essential surgical, medical, optical, dental and other remedial treatment, care, and attention: and
(b)	an adequate funeral upon his death.
It goes on to state in this act that they will have a certain means test, of course, and that the social service officers will decide, through the minister of health and welfare, who shall come under the act. They even have an appendix to the act stating what are reasonable amounts for fuel, food, and so on. Saskatchewan has one of these social security acts, and I am sure other provinces have also.
So this is a statement which the hon. member has just drawn from out of the blue without any backing whatsoever. Our people in Manitoba do not particularly need any assistance, whatever the other provinces may need, in so far as unmarried women and widows of the age of 60 are concerned.
In the field of federal social security we have also passed an amendment to the unemployment relief and assistance act and it shows in the annual report for 1959 that after this amendment was passed we had almost a doubling of the amount of unemployment assistance from December of 1958 to January of 1959. I am sure that a great many of these people were 65 years of age. I will admit that. But there are a great many people who have come under this act and who have been helped by the federal government.
I wish to remind hon. members of the opposition of the words of their leader who stated something that I think they examine every time they go through a convention. It was put on the record on July 4, 1960, at page 5666. This is what he said, as reported in Hansard:
May I conclude, Mr. Speaker, with one or two very general and very short observations. In recent years the asserted claims of the individual on the state have been matched by his protests against the state's interference in his activities and in his private life, an interference which his own demands have made easier and in some cases inevitable. The state cannot provide services and support for the citizen without acquiring the power

and authority which is necessary and desirable for that purpose. Put it another way; more social security, desirable and even necessary though that is, may often be the means to greater state powers, and the latter persistently press against the freedom and rights of citizens who are to benefit from these powers.
It is true, that the citizens who receive this social security are helped, as indeed many of them should be helped, but those citizens who have to pay for it should have some representation in this House of Commons and should have someone to speak for them. I think the words of their leader should be taken well to heart by members of the opposition, namely that if you ask for social security you must ask for control. If, for example, this resolution was passed, there would in fact be some control over the employment of women who had reached the age of 60. We know that many of these women are deserving. Notwithstanding that, many are covered at the present time by provincial statutes and many, too, are quite capable of carrying on their work past the age of 60. They have many years of good work still within their power. So although I say that I am in favour of a resolution which specifies help where there is need, I certainly am not in favour of this resolution as it is presently worded.

and I am afraid there have been few occasions in the history of this country when such a situation existed. However, I should like to make it clear that we support this measure only as a stopgap measure and not as a real answer to the situation. In fact, this is just another patch on the leaky tire of our social legislation in this country.
I believe the solution to this problem is one which we have suggested many times in this house, namely the implementation of a portable pension plan with some kind of joint survivorship clause so that if a woman should reach the pensionable age while single the pension for which she had worked all her life could be granted to her. If, on the other hand, the woman concerned was left a widow, her husband having worked over the years, then through this portable pension plan capable of being carried from job to job, and through the joint survivorship clause in the plan, her financial difficulties would be overcome and there would be no need to add another patch to the worn-out old tire of our social legislation, I think the fact that we have so many of these resolutions, each dealing with a certain weakness, a certain fault in our present social legislation, only bears out our contention that it is time we really tackled this job and came up with a satisfactory over-all solution to it.

for Fort William, and will agree that he has kindly intentions. I think that all members will agree that the question is whether or not the action suggested would, in fact, improve the situation in any way. There is already in existence a network of programs which meet the objectives toward which this particular proposal is directed. I think that an examination of some of these programs will substantiate this statement. I intend, if I can, to cover each one in the brief time at my disposal.
First of all, I want to say that those who have been very active in social welfare work over the years feel very strongly that the administrative machinery providing social aid should remain as flexible as possible. This flexibility has been provided by the various types of legislation, both provincial and federal, which are already on the books. I am not here to say that the legislation which is already on the books goes far enough. Certainly, improvements can be made. However, when we come to look at the resolution perhaps we will have to take into account some of these other programs.
The programs that are in existence already cover such things as old age assistance, blind allowances, disability allowances and the federal unemployment assistance act. The last of these measures is designed to give assistance to the provinces on these very points referred to in the resolution. This act has been amended since we came into office and I should like to remind my Liberal friends that it is a particularly progressive piece of legislation which helps the provinces and the municipalities carry out this essential work of assistance to those in need, no matter what their age may be, no matter whether they are married or unmarried or whether they are widows. When you are dealing with social problems, surely need is the criterion. We must look after those in need first.

The federal government reimburses the provinces for the payment made within the existing provincial framework of assistance. The scale on which the aid is given is determined by the provinces themselves. It is the provinces that determine the amount of aid, how it shall be given and to whom it shall be given.
I should remind hon. members that today Canadians throughout all the ten provinces
Business of the House
benefit from legislation which the Conservative government brought into effect improving the former unemployment assistance act. I should like to turn to some of the assistance programs that exist in the provinces to show what has already been done and what is already available. I should like to point out, very rapidly, that in each province there is now assistance for women of 60 or over who qualify for it on the basis of need.
Before we go any further with this matter of providing aid we will have to discuss the situation with the provinces and get their concurrence. Flexibility has been the demand of the provinces because the provinces have jurisdictional rights over this particular form of aid. The provinces demand that they shall have the right to determine to whom these funds shall go and how much shall go to each person in the various categories. The provinces are the ones that have this right and they do not intend to have their powers usurped by a resolution proposed by the hon. member for Fort William or anybody else.
I should like to mention some of the provisions that exist in the province of Ontario. Women of 60 years of age and over may qualify for general assistance or an incapacitation allowance up to $60 a month under the general welfare assistance act. This assistance is administered by the municipality and rates are in accordance with the scale set by the province. The province reimburses the municipality for 80 per cent of the amount of assistance given. The rate of general assistance for a single person living alone is $48.50 for food, clothing, household sundries, fuel allowance for cooking with electricity and shelter. Extra allowance is made for special diets, fuel or shelter under special circumstances. This is an outline of the Ontario program. The program in Manitoba is slightly different and in Saskatchewan slightly different again. However, I point out that each of the provinces insist that they shall have the right to say how much and to whom these payments shall go.
